Greedy means wanting more than you need, more than is fair, or more than is reasonable — and usually being unwilling to share what you have with others.

The key idea is excess desire combined with selfishness. It's not just about wanting something (everyone does that — it's human). Greedy carries a specific judgment: that your desire has crossed a line, that you are taking or seeking more than your fair share, often at the cost of others.

Think of it this way: if there are five slices of pizza for five people, and you take three slices for yourself without hesitation, you are being greedy. You're prioritising your own desire over the basic fairness of the situation.

The word almost always involves two elements together:

  1. Excessive desire — wanting far more than you actually need
  2. Selfishness — not caring that others might go without

Remove the selfishness, and you might just be enthusiastic or ambitious. Remove the excess, and you're just a normal person with normal wants. Greedy requires both.
What Can People Be Greedy For?

Greedy isn't only about food. It applies to almost anything a person can desire:

  • Money and wealth — This is the most common use. A greedy businessman might exploit workers, charge unfair prices, or hoard profits — not because he needs more money to survive, but purely because he wants more. This type of greed is also called avarice.
  • Food — A greedy eater takes the biggest portions, finishes food meant for others, or keeps eating long past being full. "Don't be greedy — leave some for your sister."
  • Power and control — A greedy politician might seek power not to help people, but simply to have authority over others. A greedy employer might micromanage every decision just to feel in control.
  • Attention and praise — Someone can be greedy for recognition, always steering conversations back to themselves, needing to be the centre of every room.
  • Material things — A person who always wants the newest, most expensive possessions, even when they already have plenty, can be described as greedy.
  • Time, resources, or opportunities — In group settings, someone who monopolises shared resources (the last word in every meeting, the credit for team work, the best projects at the office) is behaving greedily.
The Moral Tone of the Word

Greedy is a negative word. It passes a moral judgment. When you call someone greedy, you're not just describing what they want — you're criticising how they want it and what they're willing to do (or ignore) in order to get it.

It implies that the person lacks self-restraint and doesn't value fairness. It suggests they have let desire override both reason and conscience.

For this reason, calling someone greedy in public or to their face is considered an insult. It's not a neutral observation.

Greedy behaviour is often driven by a deep fear of not having enough, or by an intense, almost compulsive need to accumulate. A greedy person often doesn't stop to think "do I actually need this?" They simply see something and want it — and then act on that want without much regard for how it affects others.

Interestingly, greedy people are often never truly satisfied. They get what they wanted, but the feeling of "I want more" returns quickly. This cycle — wanting, getting, wanting more — is central to the idea of greed.

The word exists on a spectrum. It can describe mild everyday behaviour or deep moral corruption:

  • Mildly greedy: "I know I'm being greedy, but I'll have one more biscuit." (Light, self-aware, often said with humour)
  • Moderately greedy: "She never contributes to the group meal but always takes the most food."
  • Seriously greedy: "The landlord raised the rent by 80% just to maximise profit, leaving families homeless."
  • Profoundly greedy: Powerful figures — dictators, corrupt officials, predatory corporations — who accumulate vast wealth and power while millions suffer.

The word fits all these situations, though the seriousness of the judgment scales accordingly.

People sometimes use greedy on themselves in a lighthearted, self-deprecating way:

  • "I had seconds and then thirds — I was so greedy!"
  • "Don't judge me, I'm being greedy tonight," (said while ordering too much food)

In these cases, the speaker is acknowledging excess humorously, not actually confessing to a moral failing. Context makes it clear it's playful.

• "The greedy landlord raised rents every six months despite making record profits."
  • "Don't be greedy — share your toys with your cousin."
  • "She gave the company fifteen years, and they let her go without a second thought — greedy to the end."
  • "He stared at the display of desserts with greedy eyes." (Here it simply means intense, eager desire — used slightly poetically)
  • "A greedy corporation will sacrifice anything for profit."

• Greedily (adverb): "He ate greedily, barely pausing to breathe."
  • Greediness (noun): "Her greediness cost her friendships."
  • Greed (noun): "Greed was his defining flaw."
Greedy means wanting more than you need or deserve, without caring that your excess comes at someone else's expense — and it is always a criticism.
